technique: time — how the poem moves through it, or holds still
lesson:
Today we work on one thing: how a poem moves through time. This poem happens in order, moment by moment, like something you watch while it occurs.

Look at the verbs. First the jay "comes down hard to the split-rail post." Then it "turns it, drops it, swears." Then "the frost on the rails goes bright all at once." Then "you're already stamping warmth back into your boots." Each action follows the one before it. The poem goes from the bird landing, to the bird working, to the light changing, to you moving.

Here is why that works on you. When actions come in order, you follow them like steps. You feel time passing because each verb replaces the last one.

Try this: write four lines where each line does one new action, in the order it would happen.

The second time through, track the order of actions and notice that "So — up!" is the last action of all.

Here is the poem.
poem:
A jay comes down hard to the split-rail post,
all racket and blue, and works a seed
it can't quite crack—turns it, drops it, swears,
tries again from a different angle, stubborn as you.
You've watched that bird fight the same acorn ten ways
and get it open on the eleventh, or give it up clean.
There's a lesson in it you keep not quite learning:
the stuck thing yields or it doesn't, and either way
the morning asks only that you keep at the turning.
Now the frost on the rails goes bright all at once,
and the jay lifts off with its prize or without it—
you're already stamping warmth back into your boots.

The same old voices sound different when you put them side by side—and there's a tune somewhere that only opens up once you're on your feet to sing it—

So — up!
